'''Arkady Gendler''' (29 November 1921 – 22 May 2017, {{langx|ru|Аркадий Хунович Гендлер}} {{Transliteration|ru|Arkadiĭ Khunovich Gendler
}}, {{langx|yi|אַבֿרהם הענדלער}} {{Transliteration|yi|Avram Hendler}}) was a Soviet and Ukrainian Yiddish-language singer, composer, and folk song collector. Born in [[Kingdom of Romania|Romania]], he lived most of his life in [[Zaporizhzhia]], Ukraine, and only became known internationally as a Yiddish singer after [[Perestroika]]. In the early 21st century he was considered a living link to the prewar Romanian and Soviet Yiddish musical worlds.<ref name="Tablet 2013">{{cite news |last1=Davidzon |first1=Vladislav |title=91-Year-Old Yiddish Rock Star |url=https://www.tabletmag.com/sections/arts-letters/articles/91-year-old-yiddish-rock-star |access-date=17 July 2023 |work=Tablet |date=7 May 2013 |language=en}}</ref><ref name="Forward obit">{{cite news |last1=Matveev |first1=Yoel |title=Acclaimed Yiddish Folksinger Arkady Gendler Dies at Age 95 |url=https://forward.com/forverts-in-english/374048/acclaimed-yiddish-folksinger-arkady-gendler-dies-at-age-95/ |access-date=23 July 2023 |work=The Forward |date=7 June 2017 |language=en}}</ref>

==Biography==
===Early life===
Arkady Gendler was born on 29 November 1921 in [[Soroca]], [[Kingdom of Romania|Romania]] (now in [[Moldova]]).<ref name="Tablet 2013" /><ref name="yidishe lider liner">{{Cite AV media notes |title=ARKADY GENDLER: YIDISHE LIDER |last=Rubin |first=Joel E. |first2=Wurbs |last2=Janina |others=[[Christian Dawid]] |date=2012 |type=booklet |publisher=Golden Horn Records}}</ref> He came from a poor Jewish family; he was the tenth child of parents Rokhl and Elkhonen; much of their extended family were tailors.<ref name="Tablet 2013" /><ref name="yidishe lider liner" /> They generally spoke Yiddish at home and Romanian anywhere else; at that time he did not yet speak Russian.<ref name="Tablet 2013" /> As a youth he was a singer in a Soroca theatre troupe along with his siblings; the group would stage at least two productions per year.<ref name="yidishe lider liner" /><ref name="Tablet 2013" /> Gendler did not receive a formal musical education, but his family was very musical and would often sing as an informal choir.<ref name="yidishe lider liner" /> He also studied Hebrew in a religious [[Talmud Torah]] school.<ref name="yidishe lider liner" /> As a youth, he met many of the important Yiddish artistic figures from the region, including [[Itzik Manger]], [[Eliezer Steinbarg]], [[Zelig Bardichever]], [[Leibu Levin]] and [[Hertz Grosbard]], and saw traveling [[Yiddish theatre]] troupes perform as well as the tenor [[Joseph Schmidt]].<ref name="yidishe lider liner" /> Gendler was already interested in politics as a child and joined a Communist youth organization at age 10.<ref name="yidishe lider liner" /> He attended a Romanian-language primary school until he was forced to drop out for lack of tuition money at age 11; after that he became a tailor.<ref name="Tablet 2013" /><ref name="yidishe lider liner" />

With the [[Soviet occupation of Bessarabia and Northern Bukovina]] his region was annexed from Romania into the [[Soviet Union]]; he continued to work as a tailor until he was drafted along with his brother Dovid in the summer of 1941.<ref name="Tablet 2013" /> His sister Brokhe was also sent to serve in a medical unit. In October 1941 Arkady was wounded by shrapnel near [[Millerovo, Millerovsky District, Rostov Oblast|Millerovo]] and sent to a rear supply detail where he became a lathe operator.<ref name="Tablet 2013" /><ref name="yidishe lider liner" /> Almost the entire rest of his family were killed by the Nazis in Soroca; only the three of them who had served in the [[Red Army]] survived.<ref name="Tablet 2013" /><ref name="yidishe lider liner" />

===Soviet Union===
After the end of the war he finished a high school degree, significantly improved his command of Russian and then studied chemistry at the [[D. Mendeleev University of Chemical Technology of Russia]] in Moscow.<ref name="yidishe lider liner" /> Rather than stay in Moscow, he accepted a position as a chemical engineer at a plant in [[Zaporizhzhia]].<ref name="Tablet 2013" /> In 1952 he moved there with his wife Beyle, where he would live for the rest of his life.<ref name="Tablet 2013" /><ref name="yidishe lider liner" /> During this time he continued to enjoy singing Yiddish informally; however, with a new policy of cultural repression there was little possibility of open or professional performances in the Soviet Union of the 1950s.<ref name="yidishe lider liner" /> Some officially-sanctioned artists still toured at times; he saw Leibu Levin, whom he knew from his childhood in Romania, perform again along with the singer [[Nechama Lifshitz]].<ref name="yidishe lider liner" /> The Soviet Yiddish musical style of those artists and others like [[Mikhail Alexandrovich]] or [[Zinovy Shulman]] had a lasting influence on him.<ref name="yidishe lider liner" /> Gendler also continued to collect Yiddish folk and theatre songs during this time.{{citation needed|date=November 2023}}
[[File:View On The City (257761535).jpeg|thumb|Zapirizhzhia in 2018]]

===Post-Soviet era===
With the advent of [[Perestroika]] he retired from work as a chemical engineer and in 1992 began to teach Yiddish in a Jewish school "Aleph" in Zaporizhzhia.<ref name="Tablet 2013" /><ref name="Forward obit" /> He was a strong believer in educating younger generations in Yiddish and passing on its rich culture to them.<ref name="Forward obit" /><ref>{{cite news |last1=Yaffa |first1=Joshua |title=Klezmer in the East Looks to the West for Guidance |work=Forward |date=23 June 2006 |location=New York |page=10 |language=en}}</ref> As well, he brought his decades of work in Yiddish song to the public. He helped found KlezFest in [[Saint Petersburg]] starting in 1997; this brought him, his singing ability and his impressive repertoire of folk songs to a wider audience. He cofounded a music ensemble in Zaporizhzhia, and was soon invited to perform at festivals in Western Europe and the United States; notably, Ellie Shapiro, producer of the Jewish Music Festival in [[Berkeley, California]], saw him perform in Saint Petersburg and invited him to the US, his first appearance there in 2000.<ref name="Forward obit" /><ref name="Tablet 2013" /><ref name="yidishe lider liner" /><ref>{{cite news |last1=Hamlin |first1=Jesse |title=Jewish Music Festival at 25: Bridging cultures |url=https://www.sfgate.com/entertainment/article/Jewish-Music-Festival-at-25-Bridging-cultures-3195497.php |access-date=23 July 2023 |work=SFGATE |date=18 March 2010 |location=San Francisco |language=en}}</ref> It was at this time that Gendler, noticing how often the same Yiddish songs were performed at festivals, began to compose his own and to perform them.<ref name="Tablet 2013" /> He made his first CD in 2000 at the Jewish Music Festival in Berkeley, titled ''My Hometown Soroke''.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Wiegand |first1=David |title=A Jewish Celebration. |work=The San Francisco Examiner |date=27 February 2000 |location=San Francisco |page=9 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Pine |first1=Dan |title=Jewish Music Festival ending era. |work=The Jewish News of Northern California⁩ |date=20 February 2015 |location=San Francisco |pages=26a–28a |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Dawidow |first1=Ari |title=Arkady Gendler / My Hometown, Soroke -- KlezmerShack review |url=https://www.klezmershack.com/bands/gendler/soroke/gendler.soroke.html |website=KlezmerShack |access-date=23 July 2023 |language=en |date=10 February 2002}}</ref> Accompanied by accordionist and singer Jeannette Lewicki, Gendler sang folk songs and pieces by Itzik Manger and Zelik Barditshever, including a previously forgotten song by Manger, as well as some of Gendler's own compositions.<ref>{{cite news |title=קאָנצערט לכּבֿוד 100סטן געבוירן־טאָג פֿונעם פֿאָלקסזינגער אַרקאַדי גענדלער ז״ל |url=https://forward.com/yiddish/478622/tribute-to-the-late-yiddish-folksinger-arkady-gendler/ |access-date=23 July 2023 |work=Forverts |date=23 November 2021 |language=yi}}</ref> Other notable international appearances were at [[Yiddish Summer Weimar]] in 2006 and 2009, on a Klezmer Cruise on the [[Dnieper]] in 2007, at [[KlezKanada]] in 2007 and at the [[Jewish Culture Festival in Kraków]] in 2010.<ref>{{cite web |title=KlezKanada: A Festival of Yiddish / Jewish Culture and the arts |url=https://klezkanada.org/wp-content/uploads/2011/02/kk07-brochure-part11.pdf |website=KlezKanada |access-date=25 July 2023 |location=Montreal |page=4 |language=en |date=2007}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Mallin |first1=Lorne |title=Klezmer Cruise on a Cultural Voyage |work=The Province |date=17 December 2006 |location=Vancouver |page=D12 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=20th JEWISH CULTURE FESTIVAL in Krakow June 25th – July 4th, 2010 REPORT |url=https://www.jewishfestival.pl/wp-content/uploads/2015/11/20FKZ_RAPORT_ang.pdf |website=jewishfestival.pl |publisher=The Jewish Culture Festival Society in Krakow |access-date=25 July 2023 |page=2 |language=en }}</ref>

In the early 2010s, the German [[Klezmer]] clarinetist [[Christian Dawid]] decided to embark on a project to record Gendler's 11 original songs with new arrangements. Dawid and his collaborators decided that the style of the accompaniment should not be a specifically Jewish or Klezmer one, but rather resembling the cosmopolitan popular music Gendler grew up with, which were reflected in his compositions.<ref name="yidishe lider liner" /><ref name="interview 2011">{{cite web |title=Christian Dawid's Oral History |url=https://www.yiddishbookcenter.org/collections/oral-histories/interviews/woh-fi-0000157/christian-dawid-2011 |website=Yiddish Book Center's Wexler Oral History Project |publisher=Yiddish Book Center |access-date=10 July 2023 |language=en |date=23 August 2011}}</ref> Dawid's arrangements were recorded with the singer and a small ensemble in [[Vienna]] in late 2011.<ref name="recording gendler">{{cite web |last1=Moore |first1=Avia |title=Recording Arkady Gendler |url=https://aviamoore.com/project/recording-arkady-gendler/ |website=aviamoore.com |access-date=13 July 2023}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Arkady Gendler – Yidishe Lider |url=http://goldenhorn.com/records/ghp038.html |website=Golden Horn Records |access-date=13 July 2023 |language=en}}</ref> A book of the songs and arrangements was also published by Golden Horn Records.<ref>{{cite web |title=Scores |url=http://arkadygendler.konsonans.com/scores.html |website=arkadygendler.konsonans.com |access-date=13 July 2023 |language=en}}</ref>

Gendler died in Zaporizhzhia on 22 May 2017 at 95 years old.<ref name="Forward obit" /><ref>{{cite news |last1=Cooper |first1=Miranda |title=Arkady Gendler, a Paragon of the Yiddish Revival Movement, Dead at 95 |url=https://www.tabletmag.com/sections/news/articles/obituary-arkady-gendler-yiddish-music-legend |access-date=23 July 2023 |work=Tablet |date=22 May 2017 |language=en}}</ref>
